Add the onion, carrots and celery with a pinch of salt and cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onion is translucent and the carrots begin to soften. Stir in the garlic and oregano and cook for 1 minute, until the kitchen smells fragrant.

Pour in the broth, add the bay leaves, salt and pepper, and nestle the chicken into the liquid. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat, then lower to a gentle simmer, partially cover and cook for 15 to 18 minutes, until the thickest part of the chicken registers 165°F (74°C).
steps.tip: Keep it at a lazy simmer with small bubbles breaking the surface. A hard boil makes the chicken tough and the broth cloudy.

steps.d: Move the chicken to a cutting board and let it cool for 5 minutes, just enough to handle. Shred it into bite-sized pieces with two forks, pulling along the grain. Fish out the bay leaves and discard them.

Bring the broth back to a simmer over medium heat and stir in the orzo. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes so it does not stick and scorch on the bottom, until it is tender with a slight bite in the center.
steps.tip: The orzo keeps drinking broth as it sits, so pull it off the heat while it still has a little chew.

steps.d: Turn off the heat and stir in the shredded chicken, spinach, lemon zest and lemon juice. Let the pot sit for 1 to 2 minutes, until the spinach has wilted to dark green. Stir in the dill, then taste and add more salt, pepper or lemon until the broth tastes bright and well seasoned.
steps.tip: Add the lemon juice in stages. Start with about two thirds, taste, and add the rest if the soup still tastes flat. Salt and acid work together, so if it tastes sour but thin, add salt rather than more lemon.

steps.d: Ladle the soup into bowls and top with extra dill and a crack of black pepper. Serve with lemon wedges and crusty bread on the side.

tips: Thighs are more forgiving than breasts. Their extra fat and connective tissue keep them juicy even if they simmer a few minutes too long, while breasts dry out quickly past 165°F.
If you plan to eat the soup over several days, cook the orzo separately in salted water and add it to each bowl. That way the pasta does not swell and soak up all the broth in the fridge.
Zest the lemons before you juice them. It is much easier on a whole lemon, and the zest carries most of the fragrant oils, so do not skip it.
Small-portion tip: serve half a portion and save the rest for later. A half bowl still counts.
storage: Refrigerate the soup in airtight containers for up to 4 days. The orzo absorbs broth overnight, so reheat it in a saucepan over medium heat with an extra 1/2 to 1 cup of broth, stirring until steaming. To freeze, make the soup without orzo and freeze for up to 3 months, then cook fresh orzo when you reheat it.
variations: Greek avgolemono style
Whisk 2 eggs with the lemon juice, slowly whisk in 2 cups of the hot broth to temper, then stir the mixture back into the pot off the heat for a creamy, silky soup.
Use rotisserie chicken
Skip the poaching and simmer the broth with the bay leaves for 10 minutes, then add 4 cups of shredded rotisserie chicken with the spinach.
Swap the pasta
Use 1 cup of long-grain rice instead of orzo and simmer it for 15 to 18 minutes, or use a gluten-free small pasta and follow the package time.
Make it gentler
Serve it warm rather than hot, and go light on the lemon on unsettled days.
Protein boost
Stir a spoonful of plain Greek yogurt into your bowl.
faq: Can I use chicken breasts instead of thighs?
Yes. Start checking them at 12 minutes and pull them as soon as they hit 165°F (74°C), since breasts dry out faster than thighs.
Why did my soup turn thick and stodgy?
The orzo kept absorbing liquid as it sat. Stir in more broth or water until it loosens, then re-season with salt and lemon.
Can I make it ahead?
Yes. Make the soup through the chicken step up to 2 days ahead, then reheat, cook the orzo and finish with lemon, spinach and dill just before serving.

title: Sticky Honey Garlic Chicken Thighs
subtitle: Golden-seared thighs simmered in honey, soy and a heap of garlic until the sauce turns glossy, sticky and dark as lacquer.
desc: Sticky, garlicky, and ready in 35.
note: Serve these over plenty of steamed rice so none of the glaze goes to waste, with some quick stir-fried broccoli or cucumber salad on the side. We would take thighs over breasts here every time, since they stay juicy through the simmer. Do not rush the sear.
intro: Here is a bold claim: boneless thighs are the most forgiving cut in your grocery store, and this sticky glaze proves it. The chicken gets a hard sear, a short simmer in honey, soy and six cloves of garlic, and a last-minute thickening that leaves every piece shiny and coated. It tastes like takeout and costs a fraction of it.

Thighs work so well because they carry more fat and connective tissue than breasts, so they stay moist even at 175°F, where collagen starts softening into gelatin. The cornstarch slurry goes in last for a reason: starch granules only swell and thicken once the sauce comes near a boil, so a brief, bubbling simmer turns thin liquid into a glaze that clings.
why: One skillet, 35 minutes
Searing, simmering and glazing all happen in the same pan, which also keeps the browned bits in the sauce.
Hard to overcook
Thighs stay tender and juicy well past the point where breasts would turn dry.
Pantry sauce, big flavor
Honey, soy sauce, vinegar and garlic are probably in your kitchen already.

steps.d: Pat the thighs very dry on both sides with paper towels. Season all over with the salt, pepper and smoked paprika. Dry chicken browns faster and splatters less, so take the extra minute here.
steps.tip: If you have 15 minutes, let the seasoned thighs sit at room temperature. The salt starts to season the meat and the surface dries a little more for a deeper sear.

steps.d: In a small bowl, whisk the honey, soy sauce, vinegar, garlic and red pepper flakes, if using, until the honey dissolves. In a separate cup, stir the cornstarch into the water until completely smooth with no lumps, and set it aside.

Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers and moves like water. Lay the thighs in smooth side down; they should sizzle loudly. Cook without moving for 5 to 6 minutes, until deep golden brown and releasing easily, then flip and cook 4 to 5 minutes more.
steps.tip: Use a 12-inch skillet or work in two batches. Crowded chicken traps steam and turns pale instead of browning.

steps.d: Lower the heat to medium and pour the sauce around the chicken, scraping up the browned bits from the pan. Let it bubble gently for 5 to 6 minutes, turning the thighs once, until the chicken reaches 175°F (80°C) inside and the sauce has reduced by about a third. The garlic should smell sweet and mellow, not raw.
steps.tip: Watch the heat closely. Honey scorches quickly, so if the sauce starts to smell bitter or darken at the edges, turn it down right away.

steps.d: Stir the cornstarch slurry again, since the starch settles fast, and pour it into the pan. Simmer for 1 to 2 minutes, spooning the sauce over the chicken, until it turns thick, glossy and coats the back of a spoon.

Take the pan off the heat and let it sit for 2 minutes so the glaze sets slightly as it cools. Scatter the green onions and sesame seeds over the top. Serve over steamed rice, spooning the extra sauce over everything.

tips: Mince the garlic by hand rather than using a press. Pressed garlic releases more of its harsh compounds and can taste sharp even after simmering, while chopped garlic stays sweeter.

If the glaze gets too thick or gluey, loosen it with 1 to 2 tablespoons of hot water. If it is too thin, simmer another minute; do not add more cornstarch without mixing it into cold water first, or it will clump.
Mix the sauce and slurry up to 3 days ahead and keep them in separate sealed jars in the fridge. Dinner becomes a 20-minute sear-and-simmer.
storage: Refrigerate the chicken and sauce together in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Reheat in a covered skillet over medium-low heat with 1 to 2 tablespoons water for 5 to 7 minutes, or microwave in 1-minute bursts, since the glaze thickens in the fridge. It freezes well for up to 3 months; thaw overnight in the fridge before reheating.
variations: Use chicken breasts
Slice 2 lb breasts into 1-inch strips, sear 2 to 3 minutes per side, and simmer in the sauce only until they reach 165°F (74°C), about 3 to 4 minutes.
Make it gluten-free
Use tamari instead of soy sauce. Everything else in the recipe is already gluten-free, including the cornstarch.
Add ginger and lime
Grate 1 tablespoon fresh ginger into the sauce and swap the rice vinegar for fresh lime juice for a brighter, zippier glaze.
faq: Can I use bone-in thighs?
Yes, but they need longer. Sear skin side down for 8 to 10 minutes, then cover and simmer in the sauce for 15 to 20 minutes, until they reach 175°F (80°C), before adding the slurry.
Why is my sauce not thickening?
It likely did not come to a real simmer after the slurry went in. Cornstarch only thickens near boiling, so turn up the heat until the sauce bubbles steadily for a full minute.
Can I make it less sweet?
Cut the honey to 1/4 cup and add an extra 1 teaspoon rice vinegar. The glaze will be slightly thinner, so simmer it an extra minute.

title: Creamy Mushroom Risotto
subtitle: Arborio rice stirred slowly into creamy, glossy risotto, deepened with porcini and crowned with deeply browned cremini and Parmesan.
desc: Earthy, creamy, worth every stir.
note: Risotto is one of the best reasons we know to stay near the stove with a glass of the white wine you're cooking with. Brown the mushrooms separately and hard, because pale, steamed mushrooms add little flavor. A crisp green salad and the rest of that bottle round out the meal.
intro: Risotto has a reputation for being fussy, and it's mostly undeserved. You don't need to stir nonstop, you just need to stay nearby, keep the broth hot, and add it a ladle at a time.

The creaminess comes from the rice itself, not from cream. Arborio grains are rich in amylopectin, a starch that washes off the surface as you stir and thickens the broth into a silky sauce. Browning the cremini hard on their own first builds savory depth, and the porcini soaking liquid adds a woodsy backbone that plain broth can't match.
why: Creamy without cream
Starch released from the arborio rice makes the sauce silky on its own.
Double mushroom depth
Dried porcini flavor the broth while browned cremini bring meaty texture.
Vegetarian main course
Vegetable broth and a rennet-free cheese keep it meat-free but hearty.

items.note: check the label if you need it gluten-free
such as Pinot Grigio or Sauvignon Blanc
use a vegetarian rennet-free Parmesan-style cheese if needed

steps.d: If using porcini, soak them in 1 cup of hot water for 10 minutes until soft and pliable, then lift them out, chop finely, and pour the soaking liquid into a saucepan with the broth, leaving any grit in the bottom of the bowl. Bring the broth to a bare simmer over low heat and keep it steaming.
steps.tip: Hot broth matters. Cold broth drops the pot temperature with each ladle, which slows cooking and makes the rice gummy on the outside before the center softens.

steps.d: Heat the olive oil and 1 tablespoon of butter in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat until the butter foams. Spread the cremini in an even layer and leave them alone for 3 minutes, then stir and cook 4 to 5 minutes more, until deep golden, smelling nutty, and the pan is dry. Season with the salt, stir in the chopped porcini, and transfer everything to a bowl.
steps.tip: Hold off on salting until the mushrooms are browned. Salt added early draws out water and they steam instead of sear.

steps.d: Lower the heat to medium and melt 1 tablespoon of butter in the same pot. Cook the onion for 4 to 5 minutes until soft and translucent, add the garlic for 30 seconds until fragrant, then stir in the rice. Toast for 2 minutes, until the edges of the grains look translucent and you hear a faint crackle.

Pour in the wine, which will hiss and steam, and stir, scraping up the browned bits, until it is almost fully absorbed, about 1 to 2 minutes. Wait until the sharp alcohol smell fades before adding any broth.

Add the hot broth one ladle (about 3/4 cup) at a time along with the thyme, stirring often and waiting until each addition is mostly absorbed before adding the next. Keep it at a lively simmer. After 18 to 22 minutes the rice should be creamy and tender, with a slight bite in the center.
steps.tip: You may not need every drop of broth. Start tasting at 16 minutes, and stop adding broth once the grains are tender with just a hint of firmness.

steps.d: Take the pot off the heat and vigorously stir in most of the mushrooms, the Parmesan, and the last tablespoon of butter for 30 seconds, until glossy and flowing. Season with salt and pepper, add a splash more broth if it looks stiff, and let it rest for 1 minute.
Spoon the risotto onto warm plates, where it should spread gently into a loose wave rather than hold a stiff mound. Top with the reserved mushrooms, parsley and extra Parmesan.

tips: Don't rinse the rice. The surface starch you would wash away is exactly what thickens the risotto.
Stop cooking when the risotto looks slightly looser than you want. It keeps absorbing liquid on the plate and thickens within a minute or two.
To get a head start for guests, cook the risotto through the wine and 2 ladles of broth, spread it on a sheet pan to cool, and refrigerate for up to 1 day. Finish with hot broth in about 10 minutes.
storage: Refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container for up to 3 days; the texture will firm up as it cools. Reheat in a saucepan over low heat with a few splashes of broth, stirring until creamy. Cold risotto also makes excellent patties, pan-fried in oil until crisp and golden, about 3 minutes per side.
variations: Peas and lemon
Stir in 1 cup of frozen peas during the last 3 minutes of cooking and finish with the grated zest of 1 lemon.
Wine-free
Replace the wine with the same amount of broth plus 1 teaspoon of lemon juice or white wine vinegar for brightness.
Chicken broth version
Use low-sodium chicken broth for a richer, more savory result. The recipe will no longer be vegetarian, and you may need less salt.
faq: Can I use another rice instead of arborio?
Carnaroli or vialone nano both work, and carnaroli holds its shape especially well. Long-grain or basmati rice won't release enough starch to turn creamy.
Why is my risotto gluey or mushy?
It was likely overcooked, stirred with cold broth, or left to sit too long before serving. Start tasting at 16 minutes and serve it the moment it is loose and glossy.
Do I really have to stir the whole time?
No. Stir often, every minute or so, to release starch and prevent sticking, but you can step away briefly between ladles.

title: Harvest Kale Salad with Apples and Pecans
subtitle: Tender massaged kale tossed with crisp apples, toasted pecans, tart cranberries and goat cheese in a shallot-maple dressing.
desc: Crunchy, tangy fall salad that holds up.
note: It is our pick for potlucks and holiday tables, because it sits happily for hours without wilting. Massaging the kale is the one step you cannot skip. Add the apples, nuts and cheese at the last minute and it will taste freshly made.
intro: Kale salad has a reputation for being chewy and punishing, but that is a technique problem, not a kale problem. A two-minute massage with dressing turns tough leaves tender, glossy and sweet. From there, it is all about contrast: crisp apple, crunchy pecans, chewy cranberries and creamy goat cheese.

Rubbing the leaves breaks down their cell walls and fibrous structure, while the vinegar and salt in the dressing start to soften them further, a bit like a quick pickle. That sturdiness is also a gift, because unlike lettuce, dressed kale does not wilt into a puddle, so this salad can sit on a buffet for hours.
why: Holds for hours
Sturdy kale stays crisp-tender long after it is dressed.
Big textural contrast
Crunch, chew and creaminess land in every forkful.
Make-ahead friendly
Dress the kale a day early and assemble at serving time.

items.note: about 10 oz, stems removed, leaves thinly sliced
such as Honeycrisp and Granny Smith, cored and thinly sliced

steps.d: Spread the pecans in a dry skillet over medium-low heat and toast for 6 to 8 minutes, shaking the pan often, until they smell warm and buttery and turn a shade darker. Tip them onto a plate to stop the cooking, let cool, then roughly chop.
steps.tip: Nuts go from toasted to burnt fast, and the pan keeps cooking them after you turn off the heat. Stay close, trust your nose, and move them to a plate right away.

steps.d: Add the olive oil, vinegar, maple syrup, Dijon, shallot, salt and a few grinds of pepper to a jar. Seal and shake hard for 20 seconds, until the dressing looks creamy and emulsified; the mustard is what holds it together. Taste and adjust with more salt or maple.

Put the sliced kale in a large bowl and drizzle with about half the dressing. Use clean hands to squeeze and rub the leaves for 2 to 3 minutes, until they darken to a deep green, shrink by about a third and feel silky rather than squeaky.
steps.tip: If you have time, let the massaged kale sit for 10 minutes. The acid keeps working and the leaves get even more tender.

steps.d: Core the apples and slice them into thin wedges or matchsticks just before assembling, so they stay crisp and bright. If you are working ahead, toss them with a squeeze of lemon juice to keep them from browning.

Add the apples, pecans, cranberries and pepitas to the kale with the remaining dressing and toss until everything is glossy. Scatter the goat cheese over the top last so it stays in creamy crumbles instead of smearing, then serve.

tips: Curly kale works, but it is tougher than lacinato. Massage it an extra minute and slice it a little finer.
Cut the kale into thin ribbons, about 1/4 inch wide. Smaller pieces tenderize faster and are much easier to eat with a fork.
Rinse the minced shallot under cold water or let it sit in the vinegar for 5 minutes before adding the rest of the dressing. It tames the harsh bite without losing the flavor.
storage: Dressed kale without the apples and cheese keeps in a covered container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Store the toasted nuts in a sealed jar at room temperature, then add them, freshly sliced apples and the cheese just before serving so everything stays crisp.
variations: Roasted squash
Add 2 cups of roasted delicata or butternut squash, cooled to room temperature so it does not wilt the kale.
Make it a meal
Top with shredded rotisserie chicken or 1 1/2 cups of cooked, cooled quinoa and add an extra tablespoon of dressing.
Pear and blue cheese
Swap the apples for ripe but firm pears and the goat cheese for crumbled blue cheese. Use walnuts instead of pecans if you like.
faq: Why do I need to massage kale?
Raw kale is tough and slightly bitter. Rubbing it with dressing breaks down its fibers, so it becomes tender, sweeter and easier to eat.
Can I make this salad ahead?
Yes. Massage the kale with dressing up to a day ahead and refrigerate it, then add the apples, pecans, cranberries and cheese right before serving.
How do I make it vegan?
Skip the goat cheese and add sliced avocado or extra pepitas for richness. Check that your Dijon is vegan, which most are.

title: Easy Apple Crisp
subtitle: Soft, cinnamon-spiced apples bubbling under a craggy oat and brown sugar topping with big, buttery clusters worth fighting over.
desc: Jammy apples, crunchy buttery oat topping.
note: We like this warm, about 30 minutes out of the oven, with vanilla ice cream melting into the juices. Do not skip the mix of tart and sweet apples. Granny Smiths keep their shape and bring acidity, while Honeycrisp adds sweetness, and together they taste far more interesting than either alone.
intro: Apple crisp is the most forgiving dessert in the fall baking lineup. No crust to roll, no lattice to weave, just sliced fruit in a dish and a topping you rub together with your fingers. It still delivers everything you want from an apple pie: syrupy spiced fruit and a golden, crunchy lid.

Cold butter is what makes the topping crisp rather than cakey. When you rub it into the flour and oats, the butter stays in separate little pieces, and in the oven the water in those pieces turns to steam while the fat browns the sugar around it, leaving crunchy, craggy clusters. The spoonful of flour in the filling matters too: it thickens the apple juices as they bubble so you get a glossy sauce instead of a watery pool.
why: Big crunchy clusters
Cold butter rubbed in by hand bakes into a craggy, golden topping.
Thick, glossy filling
A little flour thickens the juices so nothing turns watery.
Easy to make ahead
Assemble it a day early and bake straight from the fridge.

items.note: about 6 to 7 medium, a mix of Granny Smith and Honeycrisp, peeled and sliced 1/4 inch thick

items.n: vanilla ice cream or whipped cream

steps.d: Set a rack in the center of the oven and preheat to 375°F (190°C). Lightly butter a 9-inch square or 2-quart baking dish and place it on a rimmed baking sheet to catch any drips.

In a large bowl, toss the sliced apples with the brown sugar, lemon juice, flour, cinnamon, nutmeg and salt until every slice is evenly coated. Spread them into the baking dish in an even layer, pressing down gently to close up any big gaps so the fruit cooks evenly.
steps.tip: Slice the apples an even 1/4 inch thick. Uneven slices cook at different rates, so you end up with some mushy pieces and some that are still crunchy.

steps.d: In the same bowl, whisk together the flour, oats, brown sugar, cinnamon and salt. Add the cold butter cubes and rub them in with your fingertips for 2 to 3 minutes, until the mixture looks like damp sand with some pea-sized clumps, then stir in the nuts if using. Work quickly so your warm hands do not melt the butter.
steps.tip: Squeeze a few handfuls together to make bigger clusters. They bake into the best crunchy bits.

steps.d: Scatter the topping evenly over the apples, all the way to the edges of the dish. Leave it loose and craggy rather than pressing it down, since a loose layer lets steam escape and bakes up crisper.

Bake for 40 to 45 minutes, until the topping is deep golden brown and the juices are bubbling thickly around the edges. A knife should slide easily into the apples in the center. If the top browns before the apples are tender, tent it loosely with foil for the last 10 minutes.
steps.tip: Look for slow, thick bubbles, not just thin juice around the edges. The flour needs to boil to fully thicken the filling, so thin bubbles mean it needs more time.

steps.d: Cool the crisp on a wire rack for at least 15 minutes so the juices thicken and the topping firms up. Serve warm with a scoop of vanilla ice cream or a spoonful of whipped cream.

tips: Freeze the butter cubes for 10 minutes before rubbing them in, especially in a warm kitchen. Colder butter stays in distinct pieces longer, which means crisper topping.
Make a double batch of topping and freeze half in a zip-top bag for up to 3 months. Sprinkle it straight from frozen over any fruit, adding a few minutes to the bake time.
If your crisp comes out soupy, the apples were likely very juicy or it was cut too soon. Next time add an extra tablespoon of flour to the filling and let it rest the full 15 minutes.
storage: Cover the crisp and keep it at room temperature for 1 day or in the fridge for up to 4 days. Reheat individual portions on a baking sheet in a 350°F (175°C) oven for about 10 minutes to bring back the crunch; the microwave warms it faster but softens the topping. You can also freeze the baked, cooled crisp, well wrapped, for up to 3 months and reheat it from thawed.
variations: Apple and berry
Swap 1 pound of the apples for 3 cups of blueberries or blackberries and add 1 extra tablespoon of flour to thicken the extra juice.
Pear and ginger
Use firm Bosc pears instead of apples and add 1 teaspoon of ground ginger to the filling.
Gluten-free crisp
Swap the flour in both the filling and topping for a 1:1 gluten-free baking blend and use certified gluten-free oats.
faq: What are the best apples for apple crisp?

Firm, slightly tart apples work best because they hold their shape. We like Granny Smith mixed with Honeycrisp, Braeburn, Pink Lady or Jonagold. Avoid soft varieties like McIntosh, which turn to applesauce.
What is the difference between a crisp and a crumble?
A crisp traditionally includes oats in the topping, which bake up crunchy. A crumble usually has a streusel of just flour, sugar and butter.
Can I make apple crisp ahead of time?
Yes. Assemble it up to 1 day ahead, cover and refrigerate, then add 5 to 10 minutes to the baking time. You can also bake it fully and rewarm it in the oven before serving.
